title: The Descent of the Call Through the Members of the Living Soul
arc: The teaching asks how far the Call must reach down to find the dispersed Living Soul, and answers by showing that the First Man is the head joining all members, set under the Father and over the Pillar of Glory, so that the Call passes through the five faculties down to the soul defiled in the Enemy and draws her back inward into the icon of her Father.
reading:
This chapter is built around a single question: when the Call of Divine Truth descends to rouse the Living Soul, how many members of that soul does it reach, and in what order does it pass through them on its way to the First Man? The answer is given not as a list but as an anatomy of the Grand Man — the Divine Human in his redemptive descent — showing that every dispersed particle of light is a member of one body, hung from one head, and reached by one summons.

The teaching first lays down the principle of organic continuity. The First Man is released forth into the natural with the members of the Living Soul attached to him as the limbs of a body hang from a head. As long as the head remains, every member, however cut or wounded, has hope; if the head were severed, the whole body would die and perish. This is the underlying logic of redemption in this chapter: the dispersed soul is not a heap of fragments but a single organism, and its survival rests entirely upon its connection to its head, the First Man — Divine Truth descending into the realm of self-love. The "house of wood" image and the body-of-flesh image are both drawn upon to make the same point: the soul-life among the members depends wholly on what stands at the top.

A second image is then layered over the first. The First Man is not only head to a body of members; he is also like the living air in which all flesh breathes. The members live not merely by structural attachment but by inhalation of his breath — that is, by perception flowing from him as the medium of spiritual life. His head, the teaching says, is laid upon the body of the Pillar of Glory in the Height of the cosmos: the Divine Human in his descent rests upon the very column of accumulated truth that rises homeward, so that every act of his reaching downward is at the same time supported by the upward axis of return.

Above the First Man stands the Father. The Father is the head over that body, the air over that Pillar, established in his holy Virgin of Light, who is the Soul of the Father and the garment he wears. Here the teaching opens the full vertical structure: the Father in his inmost Divine, clothed in the uncorrupted receptivity of Divine Wisdom; the First Man as head upon the Pillar; the members of the Living Soul hanging from him; and below, the cosmos in which those members lie scattered. The "blessed Man who is glorious" remains hidden in his icon, his form, his love, and his Virgin — that is, the Divine remains inwardly intact in pure reception even while its truth-power descends into the mingling.

It is along this entire structure that the five faculties are named: mind, thought, teaching, counsel, and reflection. These are the discrete degrees by which the Call travels from inmost rationality down to outermost discrimination. Those who raised these faculties up are said to have sent them forth — the descent of the Call is itself the sending of the soul's own intellectual structure into the place where it is needed. The Call follows "his purpose of heart"; the faculties walk after it, tracking the soul that has gone slack among the bewildered. What they find is the Living Soul lying among the lost in the likeness of the members of her body and of the cosmos itself — for the dispersed soul has taken on the shape of the world it fell into, and that very correspondence is what allows the faculties to recognize her members one by one.

The closing movement is the answering. The time of sending becomes the time of finding: the Call discovers her in the Virgin of Light, where she pleads and prays for power, peace, and the beautiful fragrance — the diffusing presence of divine love. The Man gives to his members the means to gather his soul inward and turn her back to her place; she is fashioned and adorned with art; the voices sent forth submerge inward and draw what had been defiled in the Enemy back into purity. The whole arc closes where it began, in the Virgin of Light, but now what was scattered has been reassembled "in the icon of their Father" — the Hearing that completes the Call.

Read as one argument, the chapter teaches that the descent of Divine Truth into the natural is not a leap into an alien place but an extension of one organic body. The Father is the head, the First Man is the head-on-the-Pillar, the five faculties are the limbs through which his life reaches downward, and the Living Soul among the bewildered is the body of those limbs in their captive state. Because the head is never severed, the Call always reaches every member; and because the icon of the Father is preserved in the Virgin of Light, every member drawn inward is restored to the same likeness from which it fell.
